title: Ethnobotany: How to Get Drugs from Plants
summary: Josh and Chuck explore ethnobotany and the history of drugs derived from plants, starting with ancient trepanation (Neolithic skull surgery) and early papyrus pharmacopeias from Egypt (Ebers-type list dated 1553 BC). They cover the 19th-century shift to synthetic chemistry, how ethnobotanists gather knowledge from indigenous healers (and the shift toward compensation and consent), and why chemists isolate and synthesize active compounds rather than relying on crude extraction. Examples include quinine (cinchona bark, tonic water and malaria), digitalis from foxglove, morphine and heroin from opium poppy (Bayer), aspirin from willow bark (salicin, Hippocrates), L-dopa for Parkinson's, and valerian root and valium. They discuss poisons as medicine: Pharaoh Mithridates-style poison research, the whiskey-for-snakebite myth tested by Brazilian researchers, antivenom made by immunizing horses, atropine from deadly nightshade as an antidote to nerve agents (sarin, anthrax-related toxin effects), tarantula venom for heart arrhythmia research at University of Buffalo, and scorpion venom (chlorotoxin) with iron oxide nanoparticles for brain cancer (glioma) in mice. The episode ends with a listener Q&A segment and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about working for a website, Huey Lewis, and introduce the topic of ancient medicine, including a memory of a Time-Life book about ancient brain surgery.

segments.title: Trepanation and early medicine
segments.summary: Trepanation, a Neolithic skull-opening procedure with notable survival rates, is described, along with the start of plant-based medicine knowledge in ancient Egypt, Sumer, China, Africa and India.

segments.title: Ancient pharmacopeias and the 19th-century divergence
segments.summary: Early written drug lists, including a papyrus dated 1553 BC listing seven drugs, are discussed. In the 19th century, synthetic chemistry increasingly replaced plant-based drugs, as shown by the first American Pharmacopeia's mostly plant-based entries.

segments.title: What is ethnobotany
segments.summary: Ethnobotany is introduced as a subdiscipline of anthropology that studies traditional plant knowledge, spurred by rainforest loss and uncontacted tribes. The hosts describe the training and fieldwork of ethnobotanists and the shift toward consent and compensation for indigenous knowledge.

segments.title: Isolating active compounds and synthesis
segments.summary: Chemists isolate and synthesize active ingredients because crude plant extracts vary in potency. Synthesis is cheaper and more consistent, and the hosts discuss whether a synthetic compound is still 'plant based'.

segments.title: Success stories: quinine, foxglove, morphine, aspirin
segments.summary: Examples of plant-derived drugs: quinine from cinchona bark for malaria and tonic water, digitalis from foxglove for heart conditions, morphine from the opium poppy that Bayer sold as heroin, and aspirin derived from willow bark salicin.

segments.title: L-dopa, valerian, and herbal supplement regulation
segments.summary: L-dopa for Parkinson's and valium derived from valerian root are mentioned. The hosts discuss that supplements are not FDA-regulated and that natural products can still be harmful.

segments.title: Plants as chemical factories and poisons as medicine
segments.summary: Plant enzymes and cells are used as catalysts and production systems for drugs. The hosts then turn to poisons, which have been studied since ancient Egypt, and the belief that every poison has an antidote.

segments.title: Snakebite myths, antivenom, and atropine
segments.summary: Brazilian researchers tested the whiskey-for-snakebite remedy and found it worsened outcomes. Antivenom is produced by immunizing horses with venom. Thomas Fraser's use of atropine from deadly nightshade as an antidote to nerve agents is discussed.

segments.title: Venom-based treatments: tarantula and scorpion
segments.summary: Tarantula venom is being studied at the University of Buffalo for heart arrhythmia, and scorpion venom protein (chlorotoxin) is being used with iron oxide nanoparticles to target brain cancer cells in mouse studies.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts answer listener questions about their office setup, dreams, favorite listener mail, and childhood books, then sign off with website and contact information.
